content: Sever's disease, also known as calcaneal apophysitis, is the most common cause of heel pain in children aged 8 to 13 years. It occurs due to inflammation of the growth plates in the calcaneus, which is the heel bone located at the back of the foot. This condition arises because the rapid growth of the bone outpaces the growth and flexibility of the calcaneal tendon, also referred to as the Achilles tendon. The condition is named after Dr. J.W. Sever, who first described it in 1912. Sever's disease is primarily caused by overuse of the heel bone and its associated tendons. This overuse is often linked to participation in sports or activities that involve repetitive heel movements, such as football, basketball, or lacrosse. It can also occur when a child begins a new sport or starts a new sports season. Excessive weight-bearing on the heel or excessive traction on the developing bones and tendons can also contribute to the condition. The prognosis for Sever's disease is favorable, as it is a self-limiting condition. It typically resolves on its own once the affected area is rested or when the bone completes its growth. The condition is not associated with long-term disability and usually subsides within 2 to 8 weeks. However, recurrence is possible, particularly at the start of a new sports season, if proper care is not taken. The symptoms of Sever's disease include: Pain or tenderness in one or both heels. Discomfort upon waking or when the heel is squeezed. Limping. Increased pain after walking or difficulty walking. Pain during running or playing sports. Treatment for Sever's disease may involve one or more of the following approaches: Ceasing sports or activities that exacerbate the condition. Elevating the heel to reduce strain. Performing stretching exercises for the hamstring and calf muscles two to three times daily. In some cases, immobilization with a cast may be necessary. Applying the R.I.C.E. protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation). Using specific stretching exercises to improve flexibility. Utilizing HTP Heel Seats for support. In certain cases, medication may be required, and a healthcare provider should be consulted. Maintain good flexibility through regular stretching exercises. Avoid excessive running on hard surfaces. Wear high-quality, well-fitting shoes that provide firm support and have shock-absorbent soles.
